pos: n. (the Synod of Ulster, 1690–1840, the governing assembly of the Presbyterian ministers of the north of Ireland)
etymology: Greek sunodos, a coming together, a way travelled in company; Ulster, the northern province of Ireland.
biblical_def: The Synod of Ulster was the governing assembly of the Presbyterian ministers planted in the north of Ireland by the Scots settlement of the early seventeenth century. Its seed was the presbytery erected at Carrickfergus in 1642 by the chaplains of the Scottish army, the first presbytery in Ireland; by 1659 there were five presbyteries, and after the Revolution of 1688 they met as one body, which from 1690 sat annually and governed the northern church for a hundred and fifty years. It was no establishment and never held the civil sword. Its ministers were sustained by their own people and by the royal bounty, and its courts had only the authority of the word, which is the only authority a church court ever truly has. The synod ordained and examined, visited congregations, planted new ones, disciplined the scandalous, and sent its deputies to the General Assembly in Scotland. The pattern was apostolic and deliberately so: “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6). Its annals are the annals of Irish Presbyterianism — the Pacific Act of 1720, the subscription quarrel that cost it the Presbytery of Antrim in 1726, the long Arian decay of the eighteenth century, and the orthodox recovery under Henry Cooke which ended in the union of 1840 and the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and a presbytery as a body of elders in the Christian church.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church.
ORDA'IN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to invest with ministerial functions.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: The assembly of the Ulster Scots, apostolic in pattern and unestablished in standing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The synod is worth knowing because it answers a charge still made against presbyterian order — that courts of review are a human invention bolted onto a congregational New Testament. The Ulster ministers had no bishop, no parliament and no endowment to lean on; they met because Scripture shows apostles and elders meeting, and they held that a minister is ordained by a presbytery and not by a congregation acting alone.

The principle to recover is the one Paul left with Titus, that a church is not finished until it is ordered: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). A synod that forgot this became, within three generations, a court that could not say what its own ministers believed.
roots_summary: Greek sunodos (G4923), a company travelling together; presbuterion (G4244), a body of elders; episkopos (G1985), an overseer.
roots_lines: Greek sunodos (G4923) — a company journeying together; Luke 2:44.
Greek presbuterion (G4244) — the body of elders, the presbytery; 1 Timothy 4:14.

“the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) — how Ulster ordained.
“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — the work of a hundred and fifty years.

pos: n. (the awakening in county Antrim, c. 1625–1633, along the Six Mile Water, the first revival among the Ulster Scots)
etymology: Six Mile Water, the river running through Antrim to Lough Neagh; Latin revivere, to live again.
biblical_def: The Six Mile Water Revival was the awakening that ran through the Scots settlements of county Antrim from about 1625, named for the river along whose banks its chief congregations lay. It began under the strange ministry of James Glendinning at Oldstone, who could preach the terrors of the law and nothing else, so that men were wounded and left without a physician; the neighbouring ministers — Robert Blair at Bangor, John Ridge at Antrim, Josias Welsh at Templepatrick, Edward Brice at Broadisland, and later James Hamilton and John Livingstone — were called in to bind up what he had broken open. From that came the monthly Friday meeting at Antrim, a whole day of prayer and preaching that drew hearers from twenty miles, and from Antrim the work spread into Down and Tyrone and across the water into Ayrshire as the Stewarton sickness. Its marks were ordinary and lasting: deep conviction of sin, families gathered to worship, Sabbaths kept, and communion seasons at which hundreds sat down. It was also, from the start, a work of the preached word rather than of method. “Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD: his going forth is prepared as the morning” (Hos 6:3). By 1633 the bishops had silenced most of its ministers, and the awakening passed into the Eagle Wing emigration and the covenanting years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revival as a renewal of attention to religion after indifference and decline.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.
AWA'KENING, ppr. Rousing from sleep, in a natural or moral sense.
CONVIC'TION, n. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge.
scriptures: Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hos 6:3
Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD: his going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.
Act 2:37
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
Isa 44:3
For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:
corruption_summary: The first Ulster awakening, begun by a wounding ministry and healed by sound ones.
corruption_paragraphs: Revival is the word most emptied by modern use. It now names a scheduled series of meetings, a style of music, or a measurable result produced by a technique, so that a church may advertise a revival in advance and hold one whether or not God comes. The Six Mile Water work shows the older and truer sense: no man planned it, no man could repeat it, and the men God used were not the men who looked likeliest.

The principle to recover is that revival is asked for and not arranged: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6). Antrim's monthly meeting was a day of prayer before it was a day of results, and when the Spirit came the ministers were busy comforting the wounded rather than counting them.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah (H2421), to live, to revive; yarah (H3384), the former rain; Greek katanussomai (G2660), to be pierced through.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to be made alive again; Psalm 85:6.
Greek katanussomai (G2660) — to be pierced, pricked in heart; Acts 2:37.

“as the latter and former rain unto the earth” (Hos 6:3) — what came to Antrim.
“they were pricked in their heart” (Act 2:37) — what Glendinning's law-preaching left behind.

pos: n. (James Glendinning, fl. 1622–1630, minister at Oldstone in county Antrim, the unlikely instrument of the Six Mile Water revival)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob, a heel-catcher, supplanter; Glendinning, a Dumfriesshire place-name.
biblical_def: James Glendinning was a graduate of Edinburgh and a native of Scotland who came over to Ulster about 1622 and was placed first at Carrickfergus, where Robert Blair judged him unfit for a town charge and advised his removal to a country parish. At Oldstone, near Antrim, he became the first instrument of the Six Mile Water revival. He had, by every account that survives, one note only. He preached the law, the wrath of God and the terrors of judgment with such force that hearers fell down in the church and went home unable to eat or sleep; and he had nothing whatever to say to a wounded conscience afterward. The neighbouring ministers were sent for to do the work he could not do, and the awakening that followed was in a real sense built upon a ministry that God used and then set aside. Glendinning himself ended badly. He fell into visions and date-setting, went off toward Rome to convert the pope, and was last heard of wandering in Asia Minor. His case is a standing warning and a standing comfort: the power is not in the vessel. “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terror as extreme fear, and zeal as passionate ardour in the pursuit of any thing.
webster_full: TER'ROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing.
EN'THUSIASM, n. A vain confidence of divine favor or communication.
scriptures: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
Act 2:37
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
corruption_summary: A one-note preacher of terrors whom God used and then laid aside.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Glendinning does, however, stand against two errors at once. He rebukes the modern pulpit that will not name wrath, for God plainly honoured the naming of it; and he rebukes the man who concludes from his usefulness that he was sound, for he was not. Scripture declines to flatter zeal on its own: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2).

The principle to recover is that law without gospel wounds without healing, and that this is a defect in the minister and not in the method of God. The letter kills and the Spirit gives life (2Co 3:6); Oldstone needed Antrim and Bangor and Templepatrick before its broken men were bound up.
roots_summary: Hebrew pattish (H6360), a hammer; Greek zelos (G2205), zeal; epignosis (G1922), full knowledge.
roots_lines: Hebrew sela (H5553) — a rock, a crag; Jeremiah 23:29.
Greek gramma (G1121) — the letter, as against the Spirit; 2 Corinthians 3:6.

“a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — the man himself.
“the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2Co 3:6) — why others had to be sent for.

pos: n. (Josias Welsh, d. 1634, minister at Templepatrick, grandson of John Knox, called the Cock of the Conscience)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshiyah, the LORD supports; Welsh, a stranger, a Briton.
biblical_def: Josias Welsh was the son of John Welsh of Ayr and of Elizabeth Knox, and so a grandson of John Knox. Deposed from his regency at Glasgow for refusing conformity, he crossed to Ulster and was settled at Templepatrick in county Antrim about 1626, in the thick of the Six Mile Water work. His people called him the Cock of the Conscience, for he had a gift of searching the heart until a man could not keep his secret from himself; and he carried into the Irish plantation the weight of mourning over his own soul that his family was known for. Livingstone, who knew him well, records that he spent whole nights in prayer and complained more of his own hardness than of any man's. He was one of the four ministers who sustained the monthly Antrim meeting, and one of the four whom Bishop Echlin silenced in 1632; he died in 1634 before the Eagle Wing sailed, worn out at about forty. His ministry was the pastoral answer to Glendinning's hammer, and it was costly to the man who gave it. “Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the internal or self-knowledge of right and wrong, and to warn as to caution against danger.
webster_full: CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong.
WARN, v.t. To give notice of approaching or probable danger; to caution.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something.
scriptures: Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
Eze 3:17
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Knox's grandson in Ulster, who searched consciences and mourned his own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The title his people gave him would be heard today as an insult, and the ministry it describes as an intrusion. A preacher whose business is to make a man uneasy about himself is now called manipulative; the assumption is that the conscience should be soothed and that whatever disturbs it has overstepped.

The principle to recover is the apostolic one that warning is part of feeding. A watchman is set to give warning from God and is answerable if he does not (Eze 3:17), and Paul's three years at Ephesus were spent warning “every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31). Welsh wept first over himself, which is what separates a searching ministry from a cruel one.

“his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jer 20:9) — the Cock of the Conscience.
“I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel” (Eze 3:17) — his charge.

pos: n. (Edward Brice, c. 1569–1636, minister at Broadisland, the first Presbyterian minister settled in Ireland)
etymology: Old English Eadweard, guardian of prosperity; Brice, from the Celtic saint's name Bricius.
biblical_def: Edward Brice was a Scot of Airth who graduated at Edinburgh, served at Bothkennar and Drymen, and fell foul of the Archbishop of Glasgow over his opposition to the intrusion of bishops into the Scottish kirk. He crossed to Ulster in 1613 and was settled at Broadisland, now Ballycarry in county Antrim, where he is reckoned the first Presbyterian minister to take a charge in Ireland. For twenty-three years he preached there, and his settlement marks the beginning of the whole northern church: the Scots who came over with the plantation found a minister of their own order waiting. He lived to see the Six Mile Water awakening touch his own parish and was one of the ministers silenced by Bishop Echlin in 1632, dying four years later with his deposition unresolved. Livingstone remembered him as a man much in the study of the covenant and plain in his dealing with souls. His career is a quiet example of how God furnishes a scattered people: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). What the planter sowed others watered, and the increase was not his to give. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to plant as to set in the ground for growth, and a pioneer as one who goes before to prepare the way.
webster_full: PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth.
PIONEE'R, n. One who goes before to remove obstructions or prepare the way.
SCAT'TER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: The first Presbyterian minister settled in Ireland, planter of the northern church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Brice is useful against a habit rather than an error: the habit of dating a church's life from its first great awakening or its first famous preacher, and forgetting the man who sat twenty years in a plain country charge before either came. Broadisland had a settled ministry for a dozen years before Oldstone was ever heard of.

The principle to recover is the division of labour Paul insists on, which forbids both envy and self-congratulation: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6). The sower goes out weeping and the sheaves come later, often to another man's arms (Psa 126:6).

roots_lines: Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad, as a sowing; Acts 8:4.
Greek auxano (G837) — to cause to grow, give increase; 1 Corinthians 3:6.

“I have planted, Apollos watered” (1Co 3:6) — Broadisland before Oldstone.
“shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6) — twenty-three years at one charge.

pos: n. (John Ridge, d. c. 1637, minister at Antrim, founder of the monthly Antrim meeting)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Ridge, from Old English hrycg, a back, a crest of land.
biblical_def: John Ridge was an Englishman, a graduate of Oxford, settled at Antrim about 1619 and reckoned by all who wrote of him the ablest head among the ministers of the Six Mile Water work. It was Ridge who proposed and sustained the monthly meeting at Antrim, held on the last Friday of each month: a whole day given to prayer and to four sermons, with the ministers of the surrounding country preaching in turn and hearers coming twenty and thirty miles. Out of that meeting the awakening was fed, ordered and kept from running wild, for the men who preached at it were teachers as well as awakeners and laid doctrine under the convictions that Glendinning had raised. Ridge himself was known for plainness and for making the sense of the text clear, in the manner of Nehemiah's Levites: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). He was silenced with his brethren in 1632, removed to Ireland's south and then to England, and died about 1637. The Antrim Friday was his monument, and it was copied afterward in Scotland and in America wherever ministers wanted an awakening taught as well as felt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conference as a meeting for consultation or instruction, and to expound as to explain or lay open the meaning.
webster_full: CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of two or more persons for conversing or consultation.
EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to interpret.
DISTINCT'LY, adv. With distinctness; not confusedly; clearly.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: The Oxford man at Antrim whose monthly Friday fed and ordered the revival.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ridge answers the common assumption that order and awakening pull against each other — that structure quenches the Spirit, so that a work of God must be left unstructured to stay genuine. Antrim was a fixed day, a fixed form and a settled rota of preachers, and it was the means by which a revival survived its own first heat.

The principle to recover is Nehemiah's: read the book distinctly, give the sense, cause the people to understand the reading (Neh 8:8). Conviction that is never taught dies, and the first Ulster converts continued “stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) because men like Ridge made that their business.

Hebrew sekel (H7922) — discretion, the sense of a thing; Nehemiah 8:8.

“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — what the meeting secured.
“the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — Ridge's reputation for plainness.

pos: n. (Robert Blair, 1593–1666, minister at Bangor and afterwards at St Andrews, chaplain to Charles I and leader of the Eagle Wing)
etymology: Old German Hrodberht, bright in fame; Gaelic blar, a plain, a field.
biblical_def: Robert Blair was regent of philosophy at Glasgow until he could no longer subscribe the ceremonies, and in 1623 crossed to Ulster, where Viscount Clandeboye settled him at Bangor in county Down. There he became, with Ridge and Welsh and Livingstone, one of the pillars of the Six Mile Water awakening and a preacher of such weight that men came from both shores to hear him. Silenced by Bishop Echlin in 1631 and deposed in 1632, he went to London to plead with the king, and when that failed he joined the attempt of 1636 to carry a ministry and a congregation to New England in the ship Eagle Wing — a voyage God turned back by storm in mid-Atlantic, which Blair read as a plain providence that Scotland was not yet done with them. Returning, he was settled at Ayr and then at St Andrews, served as a commissioner to the Westminster Assembly, was chaplain to Charles I, and laboured to hold the Resolutioners and Protesters together. Ejected again in 1661, he died at Couston in 1666. His own account of the revival is the chief source we have for it. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines boldness as courage, and to persuade as to influence by argument or entreaty.
webster_full: BOLD'NESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; confidence.
PERSUA'DE, v.t. To influence by argument, advice, intreaty or expostulation.
PROV'IDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Dan 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: Bangor's preacher, leader of the Eagle Wing, and the revival's own historian.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Blair's life does rebuke a reading of providence common in our own day, in which a thwarted plan is treated as evidence of unbelief or of insufficient resolve. The Eagle Wing carried godly men on a godly errand and was driven back by weather; Blair did not conclude that he had lacked faith, but that God had another use for him at home.

The principle to recover is that the arm of flesh is never the engine, even in a work plainly blessed: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). The men whom Antrim's hearers marvelled at were marvelled at for the same reason as Peter and John — because they had been with Jesus (Act 4:13).

roots_lines: Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; Acts 4:13.
Hebrew zahar (H2094) — to shine, to warn; Daniel 12:3.

“they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13) — what hearers saw in the Antrim preachers.

pos: n. (John Livingstone, 1603–1672, minister at Killinchy and Ancrum, preacher of the Kirk o' Shotts)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Livingstone, from a Lothian place-name.
biblical_def: John Livingstone was licensed in Scotland, could find no settlement because he would not conform, and in 1630 was ordained at Killinchy in county Down by the Ulster brethren, among whom he spent the richest years of his ministry. He is best remembered for a single day. At the communion at Shotts in June 1630, after a night the ministers spent in prayer and a morning in which he had fled the churchyard feeling wholly unfit, he preached in the open air from Ezekiel on the dry bones and about five hundred professed to be converted under that one sermon — the Kirk o' Shotts, the most famous day in Scottish revival history. He returned to Killinchy, was silenced in 1632, sailed in the Eagle Wing and came back with Blair, served afterward at Stranraer and Ancrum, sat in the Westminster Assembly's dealings as a Scottish commissioner, and was banished to Rotterdam in 1663 for refusing the oath of allegiance, dying there in 1672. His Memorable Characteristics is our best portrait of the Ulster ministers. Of Shotts he would say only what Ezekiel was told: “Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man” (Eze 37:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to prophesy as to utter predictions or to preach, and conversion as a change from one state to another, particularly a turning to God.
webster_full: PROPH'ESY, v.t. To foretell future events; to preach; to instruct in religious doctrines.
CONVER'SION, n. A change of heart from a state of sin to a state of holiness.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; concord; the celebration of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: Eze 37:9
Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Act 4:31
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The preacher of the Kirk o' Shotts, Killinchy's minister and the revival's best witness.
corruption_paragraphs: Livingstone's day at Shotts is the text most often misused in revival literature, pressed into service as proof that if a preacher will only prepare in a certain way, or feel a certain way, five hundred souls may be expected. He himself recorded the opposite: he had run from the place, judged himself unfit, and preached because he could not honourably escape.

The principle to recover is that the breath is commanded and does not come at call. Ezekiel preached to a valley of bones and was told to prophesy to the wind (Eze 37:9); the three thousand at Pentecost were added by God after the same kind of praying that left the Shotts ministers on their knees all night, and the place that was shaken was shaken when they had prayed (Act 4:31).
roots_summary: Hebrew ruach (H7307), wind, breath, spirit; naba (H5012), to prophesy; Greek prostithemi (G4369), to add.
roots_lines: Hebrew naba (H5012) — to prophesy, speak as a prophet; Ezekiel 37:9.
Greek prostithemi (G4369) — to add to a number; Acts 2:41.
usage: “Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man” (Eze 37:9) — his text at Shotts.
“there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41) — the pattern he appealed to.
“when they had prayed, the place was shaken” (Act 4:31) — the night before the sermon.

pos: n. (Henry Cooke, 1788–1868, minister in Belfast, who drove Arianism out of the Synod of Ulster)
etymology: Old German Heimerich, ruler of the home; Cooke, an occupational surname.
biblical_def: Henry Cooke was born in county Londonderry, educated at Glasgow, and settled at last in Belfast, where for forty years he was the dominant figure in Irish Presbyterianism. He found the Synod of Ulster honeycombed with Arianism, the fruit of a century in which men had been licensed without being asked what they believed; the non-subscription party held that to require assent to the Westminster Confession was to put a human document over Scripture, and under that plea the deity of Christ had quietly ceased to be preached in many pulpits. Cooke forced the question into the open. In the synods of 1827 to 1829 he pressed for examination of candidates on the doctrine of the Trinity, carried the house, and the Arian ministers withdrew in 1830 to form the Remonstrant Synod. He went on to lead the union of 1840 that created the General Assembly, to defend the Presbyterian colleges, and to contend in public against O'Connell and against Rome. He was a controversialist by calling and knew it. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13), was in effect the whole of his programme.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subscription as the act of signing one's name in attestation, and Arianism as the doctrines of Arius, who denied the divinity of Christ.
webster_full: SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation.
A'RIANISM, n. The doctrines of the Arians.
OR'THODOX, a. Sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
corruption_summary: The Belfast minister who made the Synod of Ulster say what it believed.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument Cooke defeated is still the standard argument against confessions: that a creed is a man-made addition, that no honest man should be bound by another century's words, and that requiring subscription is narrow. Ulster had run that argument for a hundred years and the result was not liberty but silence — congregations that could not learn from their own pulpits whether Christ is God.

The principle to recover is that a form of sound words is itself commanded (2Ti 1:13), and that an elder is to be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). A church with nothing to subscribe has nothing to examine a candidate by, and nothing to depose a heretic for.
roots_summary: Greek hupotuposis (G5296), an outline, pattern; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; antecho (G472), to hold fast.
roots_lines: Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, form, pattern; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy; Titus 1:9.
usage: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — his case for subscription.
“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) — the synods of 1827–29.
“Fight the good fight of faith” (1Ti 6:12) — forty years in Belfast.

pos: n. (James Seaton Reid, 1798–1851, minister at Carrickfergus and historian of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob; Reid, Scots for red, red-haired.
biblical_def: James Seaton Reid was minister at Donegore and then at Carrickfergus, afterwards professor of ecclesiastical history at Glasgow, and the man who gave Irish Presbyterianism its memory. His History of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, the first volume published in 1834, was built on the synod's own minutes, on state papers, and on the manuscript accounts of Blair and Livingstone which he was among the first to use carefully; it remains the standard narrative of the plantation ministers, the Six Mile Water revival, the silencings, the Antrim non-subscription breach and the Arian century. He wrote as a believing historian and not as an antiquary: his aim was that a church then recovering its confession should know what it had been and how it had come so near to losing the gospel. He died at Lisburn in 1851 with the third volume unfinished, and it was completed by W. D. Killen. The labour he undertook is the labour Scripture lays on every generation of a covenant people: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of facts and events in the order in which they happened, and a record as a register or authentic memorial.
webster_full: HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states.
REC'ORD, n. A register; an authentic or official copy of any writing.
ANNALS, n. A history of events in the order of time.
scriptures: Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
corruption_summary: The historian who gave Irish Presbyterianism its memory, from the synod's own minutes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Reid's work does stand against a method, now common, which treats a church's own records as evidence only of what the church wished to believe about itself, and the historian's task as the exposure of that wish. Reid read the minutes as records of real courts, real men and real repentance, and corrected them where the state papers contradicted them.

The principle to recover is that remembrance is a duty laid on the church and not an indulgence: what God has done is to be written for the generation to come (Psa 102:18), and “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). A church that forgets the Arian century will run it again.
roots_summary: Hebrew sippur from saphar (H5608), to recount, declare; dor (H1755), a generation; Greek charis (G5485), grace.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to recount, declare, number; Psalm 145:4.
Hebrew dor (H1755) — a generation, an age; Psalm 102:18.
usage: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — why he wrote.
“This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — three volumes from the minutes.
“by the grace of God I am what I am” (1Co 15:10) — his verdict on the fathers he recorded.
